rootCauses.claim: The web fonts are only requested after the first layout finds text that uses them. They then reach the main thread in the middle of the intro, and each arrival invalidates every text object, so the whole page is laid out again.
rootCauses.evidence: Warm trace: BeginRemoteFontLoad for Inter @209, Inter Tight @287 and JetBrains Mono @540 (the requests start only when layout needs them). JetBrains Mono's response is held behind the 521ms task and is delivered @986 (RemoteFontLoaded). InvalidateSubtreeForFontUpdates fires @989 and the 987 task then runs Layout 66ms with dirty 1115/1176. Cold trace: the fonts are requested @503/587/631 but delivered @1685-1687 (blocked behind the 858ms script.js evaluation). InvalidateSubtreeForFontUpdates fires @1704, and the 1702 task (273ms) contains a FireAnimationFrame of 184ms with Layout 157ms dirty 1300/1372, forced by update@script.js:909, plus about 107ms of Paint. In both traces the hero text was first painted after the fonts had arrived, so the swap has no visible benefit. It only costs a full relayout. A re-trace confirmed it (CPU was contended, so only the ordering matters): baseline cold showed a font invalidation @3309 followed by a second full Layout of 305ms (1300/1372). With the preload, the only font invalidation is @537 while the DOM is still small, and only one full layout happens.

rootCauses.claim: boot.js is deferred and runs right before DOMContentLoaded, when the whole DOM already exists. Its document.body.classList.add('ready') (boot.js:13) recalculates style for the entire page in the middle of the intro, even though the splash is switched off and the class changes nothing on screen. rootCauses.evidence: Warm trace: EvaluateScript boot.js @1902.3, then ScheduleStyleRecalculation with stack DOMTokenList.add < boot.js:13 @1903.9, then UpdateLayoutTree 82.2ms with elementCount 1077 @1928 (the long task @1908, 104ms, together with the 19.5ms beacon eval). rootCauses.claim: assets/visits.json is downloaded twice on every load: two identical fetch() calls with cache:'no-cache'.
rootCauses.evidence: script.js:830 and script.js:862. Trace: two High-priority ResourceSendRequest for assets/visits.json @1446 (warm) and @1382/1383 (cold), both 9474 bytes. FPS cost is negligible, but it is a real duplicate download.

rootCauses.claim: The biggest entry cost (~433-462ms first full layout) comes from incremental rendering of a partly parsed document plus the size of the DOM, not from image or network loading. The loading lane cannot remove it without delaying first paint.
rootCauses.evidence: Warm: ParseHTML chunks @135 (L0), 253 (L101), 388 (L232), 446 (L308-1023), 1147 (L1023), 1421 (L1111 = script.js). Each chunk is followed by a frame that lays out the whole partial DOM: Layout 32/72/20/433/64ms, with dirty 7, 132, 201, 977/1176 and 153/1300. investigations.notes:
I did not edit the repo; git status shows only the user's pre-existing changes (assets/visits.json, scripts/fetch-visits.js).

Everything for this lane is in fixes/loading/:

- make.js: rebuilds every modified copy from the pristine repo files, keeping CRLF.
- index.fontpreload.html, index.earlyready.html, index.combined.html, boot.js, script.earlyready.js, script.combined.js: the modified copies.

Harness problems that will hit the orchestrator:
1. The shared bench.js 'visual' hangs on the current page. shot() waits for every !complete image, and 15 loading=lazy testimonial avatars below y≈2900 never load. I used a local copy (fixes/loading/bench.js) that skips lazy images below y=1800 and has an 8s cap.
2. During my run the static server on :5173 refused connections (curl 000, only TIME_WAIT sockets). I did not restart it. My local bench copy serves every localhost request from the repo on disk through puppeteer interception, read-only, with 'files' overrides applied as in the shared harness. External hosts (Google Fonts, jsdelivr, Cloudflare) still go to the network. 'timing' needs the server back up, or the same interception.
3. The visual diffs at 900/1400ms are the hero JS count-up still running when the screenshot is taken. With a 3.2s settle (fixes/loading/bench_settled.js) both noise and all variants come out at exactly 0.

Trace artifact: the 113ms warm task at 1273ms is LayerTreeHost teardown from the warm-up tab. It is not a user cost.

Rejected, with evidence:
- decoding="async" on the hero imgs. Decode is already off the main thread and cheap: 24 ImageDecodeTask of 1-2ms each on worker threads. async could let frames commit without the image, which means later pop-in.
- fetchpriority or preload for the hero thumbnails. All 26 files finish before the rows are first laid out: 248ms vs 270ms warm, 527ms vs 557ms cold. Nothing pops in today.
- loading=lazy on the duplicate track halves. Same URLs, so they are memory-cache hits and add no bytes. Lazy would risk pop-in as the track scrolls.
- defer on script.js. Deferred scripts run in document order, so boot.js would run before script.js. The count-up would then start earlier, and the parse would not get shorter.
- Delaying the Cloudflare beacon. 20-28ms of eval is not a long task once the 82ms recalc is gone, and delaying it risks losing analytics.
- Moving the head inline scripts above the Google CSS link. In the cold trace this unblocks the parser at about 282ms instead of 435ms, but first paint stays blocked by the CSS and the first layout would just get bigger.
- rel=expect blocking=render. It would delay first paint and change what is on screen.

The big ~433-462ms first full layout is DOM size plus incremental rendering of a partly parsed page. It belongs to the offscreen-work and forced-layout lanes.

Interaction with other lanes: loading-early-ready changes only section 5a of script.js (line 454). A boot.css selector fix from the style-invalidation lane for the same 82ms recalc is compatible with it.

Follow-up the user could choose: self-host the 3 woff2 files and inline their @font-face rules. That removes the third-party render-blocking css2 request (24KB, which in the cold trace arrived about 155ms after styles.css) and the version-drift risk of the preload URLs. It needs the files downloaded into the repo, so I did not do it.

rootCauses.claim: script.js#loop@937 (section 6c, the scroll-driven gradient loop) looks like the biggest rAF cost, but it isn't. Its 1905ms of FireAnimationFrame (warm) is almost all the per-frame style recalc that the CSS animations need anyway, and the loop's getBoundingClientRect only runs it early. Removing the loop saves almost nothing.
rootCauses.evidence: In trace_warm, loop@937 has 134 calls, 1905ms total, and 1738ms of that is forced UpdateLayoutTree with stack script.js:910 (rect read). Each forced recalc covers about 168 elements (e.g. 3252.7ms: 17.5ms, elems=168), and the lifecycle UpdateLayoutTree in the same frame has elems=0. I ran a probe with loop@937 disabled: the same ~159 elements per frame are then recalculated in the lifecycle (5725 elems over 36 recalcs in 3.5-4.5s), so the work moves rather than disappears. Invalidation tracking for 2.5-3.5s shows every dirty element is reason 'Animation': FIGURE.quote float (84 per second, offscreen), .particle 56, I 35, .bg-row-track 32, .dot.pulse 18 (box-shadow), .price-card 18 (offscreen), .accent-orbs 12 (background-position), .btn-shiny (--gradient-angle), .scroll-line (transform-origin), .cfooter-aurora/.cfooter-marquee-track (offscreen). These belong to the style-invalidation and offscreen-work lanes.

rootCauses.claim: The nav-pill driver (script.js:1092-1120) writes --nav-pill, --nav-bar-vis and --nav-pill-vis on <html> during script init. The values are 0.000/1.000/0.000, which equal the :root defaults in styles.css:3003-3007, but the write still triggers a style recalc of the whole document. The same whole-document recalc then happens on every scroll frame between 0 and 360px.

Right after the root writes, the next layout read (testimonials getBoundingClientRect, script.js:1258) forces UpdateLayoutTree with elems=1035 and 97.0ms. Cold trace: elems=1035, 92.9ms at 1456ms. Both sit inside the 351ms script.js evaluation long task at 1421ms. Only rules inside .nav read these variables (styles.css:3016-3068). Adding .scroll-fade (which declares --leave:0) invalidates every section subtree. update() then writes '--leave: 0.000', equal to that default, on each section, with a getBoundingClientRect between writes, so each section gets an extra forced full-subtree recalc. The footer's first --fp=0.000 write (script.js:1239) repeats the pattern on the 44-element footer.
rootCauses.evidence: Warm trace, forced at script.js:975: the first read is elems=660 (78.4ms, mostly the scroll-fade subtrees). It is followed by elems=23 (2.4ms), 65 (5.9ms), 408 (38.8ms) and 98 (9.1ms), then elems=47 (4.3ms) forced by the rail at script.js:1029. That is 60.5ms of extra recalcs (57.9ms cold). The footer --fp write is followed by a 44-element recalc of 4.3ms at 1829ms. With @property --leave set to inherits:false, the 660-element recalc drops to elems=40 (8.2ms) and the chain drops to elems=2 each (about 0.2ms). With write-on-change, the chain disappears. All of this happens before first interaction, inside the script-eval long task.

It writes an inline background-image on the parent .accent/.accent-soft that is never visible, because styles.css:3837-3846 sets 'background-image: none !important' on it. It reads the second element's rect after writing to the first, which forces an extra small recalc. It also runs querySelector and closest for every element on every frame.

Invalidation tracking shows 'Inline CSS style declaration was mutated | SPAN.accent | script.js:931'. rootCauses.claim: The other per-frame callbacks are cheap, and Blink already skips writes that don't change anything. That is why 'write only on change' pays off only where the first write differs textually from the stylesheet default (the three cases above).
rootCauses.evidence: Warm trace FireAnimationFrame totals: tick@424 (hero counters) 208 calls, 49ms. smooth-scroll.js#loop@32 (idle Lenis raf) 131 calls, 24ms. tick@1296 (lite FPS probe) 39 calls, 5.9ms. update@1230 (footer) 1 call. Once the hero gradient converges (3333-3463ms), the elems=2 recalc no longer appears, so Blink is skipping identical inline-style writes. The same is true of identical textContent writes (Node::setTextContent fast path). The counter tick does replace its Text node on every value change ('Node was inserted into tree #text script.js:429'), but that costs only about 1.2-1.6ms of layout per frame at 4x.

candidates.title: Stop no-op init writes of scroll-driven custom properties, scope the nav vars to #nav, and register --leave as non-inherited
candidates.mechanism: This is C1 (script.js) plus C2 (styles.css). (a) The nav pill driver remembers the last values it wrote, starting from the :root defaults (0, 1, 0), and writes only when a value changes. It writes on #nav instead of <html>, so a change recalcs about 20 nav elements instead of about 1035. (b) The section fade remembers the last --leave per section, starting at '0.000' (the .scroll-fade default). It reads all rects first and writes afterwards. (c) The footer --fp is written only on change, starting at '0.000'. (d) The gradient loop drops the invisible parent write, caches the .accent-text child and the hero flag, reads both rects before writing, and writes only when the gradient string changes. (e) The CSS adds '@property --leave {syntax:<number>; inherits:false; initial-value:0}', so adding .scroll-fade and writing --leave recalc only the section itself and not its subtree. Measured structurally (elementCount per recalc): the init 1035-element root recalc, the 23/65/408/98/47 chain and the 44-element footer recalc are gone, and the 660-element scroll-fade recalc drops to 40. Estimated saving inside the 351ms script.js long task at about 1.4s: about 230ms warm at 4x (97 + 60.5 + ~70 + 4.3), about 205ms cold. Scrolling 0-400px: 0 whole-document recalcs instead of 42.
candidates.visualIdentity: What is drawn does not change. Every value skipped equals the CSS default it would have overwritten ('0.000' vs 0, '1.000' vs 1), and those properties are only used inside calc(), so the used values match. The skipped parent background-image is overridden by !important, as getComputedStyle 'none' confirms. In the gradient loop the reads and the lerp happen in the same order with the same inputs; background-image does not change geometry, so reading rects before writing returns the same numbers. Blink already skipped identical writes. --leave is read only by .scroll-fade itself (styles.css:263-266), so making it non-inherited changes nothing that a descendant reads. Checked with a computed-state probe: nav pill, section opacities and --fp are identical at 10 scroll positions, and /#pricing lands at y=4549 with pricingTop=80, isPill=true, padding 10px, as in baseline.
risks: Future CSS outside .nav that reads var(--nav-pill / --nav-bar-vis / --nav-pill-vis) would see only the :root defaults while scrolling. Today only .nav rules read them (styles.css:3016-3068). Also, getComputedStyle(document.documentElement) no longer reflects the live nav values; nothing reads them.

The skip-at-init logic assumes the CSS defaults stay .scroll-fade{--leave:0}, :root{--nav-pill:0;--nav-bar-vis:1;--nav-pill-vis:0} and .cfooter{--fp:0}. If someone changes a default, the matching JS initial value has to change too (comments in the code point to this).

@property --leave with inherits:false: a future descendant rule that uses var(--leave) would get 0. Making --leave a typed <number> also makes it animatable, which would matter only if a .scroll-fade element ever gets 'transition: all' (today the transitions list opacity, filter and transform explicitly). Browsers without @property ignore it, which is the same as today.
The gradient loop caches the .accent-text child at init. If JS ever replaced that child at runtime, the cached reference would go stale (nothing does this today).

rootCauses.claim: Paint is not the main entry cost. The '120-155ms Paint' figures in the brief come from adding up nested Paint events. The actual top-level paint inside those long tasks is 37ms (task at 987ms), 32ms (at 1787ms) and 15ms (at 2302ms). Across the whole entry window, paint plus compositing on the main thread is about 18% of busy time; layout, style and script are about 75%.
rootCauses.evidence: trace_warm.json, renderer main thread 9600:16248, only outermost events counted (fixes/paint-composite/tr4.js, tr8.js). Over 0-3500ms: RunPaintLifecyclePhase 467ms in 42 frames, made of Layerize 236, Paint 175, PrePaint 107. Commit adds 72. For comparison: UpdateLayoutTree 1054, Layout 761, FireAnimationFrame 570, all main-thread RunTask 3240. Chrome emits one Paint event per painted paint layer, all nested inside the #document Paint, so summing every Paint event inflates the number about 4x. Raster does not run in the renderer. With out-of-process raster it runs in the GPU process: CrGpuMain shows RendererRasterWorker 713ms and SkiaOutputSurfaceImplOnGpu::FinishPaintRenderPass 581ms in 0-3.5s. That process is not CPU-throttled and runs in parallel. The brief's '~120ms off-main raster' counted only RasterTask/ImageDecodeTask, so it missed this.

rootCauses.claim: The biggest paint/composite cost on each frame is a full re-layerization (PaintArtifactCompositor::Update, shown as 'Layerize'). It runs on about 95% of frames and takes about 6ms of each ~30ms frame at 4x. Two things cause it. (a) The four price-card float animations (composited 'translate', styles.css:3145-3163) run even while the section is far off-screen, and nothing gives them a paint-containment boundary. (b) The status-dot 'pulse' and 'pulseGreen' rings grow their box-shadow spread from 0 to 10px (styles.css:426-429 and 3500-3503), which changes the dot's paint bounds on every frame.
rootCauses.evidence: In trace_warm, 133 of 140 Layerize events are full PaintArtifactCompositor::Update. In steady state Layerize is 168ms per second at 4x. I isolated each animation (all others paused, background-image JS writes stubbed) and counted full updates per frame, using thread CPU time (tdur) to stay robust against CPU contention. Price-card floats only: 18 of 20 frames. Quote floats only: 0 of 22 frames; the quotes run the same kind of translate float but sit inside .tcols, which already has contain:paint (styles.css:3762). Pulse dots only: 18 of 64. Accent orbs only: 0 of 121. btn-shiny only: 0 of 88; these two repaint every frame but take the cheap repaint-only path. Price floats plus pulse: 15 of 27. Adding #pricing{contain:paint} plus a transparent fixed-size ring: 0 of 31. Full page, baseline: 49/49, 40/41, 46/46 and 25/31 frames, Layerize CPU median 1.5-2.4ms per frame. Full page with the fix: 8/62, 7/61, 8/33 and 9/40, median 0.2-0.4ms. LayerTree polling of the baseline also shows layers being created and destroyed (172-175 layers, up to 5 structural changes in 2s). That churn is gone with price floats paused or with contain:paint.

rootCauses.claim: The whole hero and nav intro runs on the main thread. Every intro keyframe animates filter: blur(), and Chrome never moves an animation that blurs onto the compositor, so the opacity and transform in those same keyframes stay on the main thread too. During load the main thread produces very few frames. The hero text and nav therefore step through about 6-8 states while the composited collage behind them keeps moving smoothly. This is the visible 'trava um pouco'.
rootCauses.evidence: In trace_warm, Animation events give compositeFailed=4096 (filter-related property may move pixels) for heroBadgeIn, heroTitleIn, 4x heroFadeIn (styles.css:626, 646, 674, 683, 703, 760), navIn (4045) and 7x navItemIn (4054). Main-thread BeginMainFrame starts between 0 and 2500ms are 127, 155, 270, 399, 987, 1172, 1387, 1787, 2012, 2065, 2302. Compositor DrawFrame is continuous at about 120Hz from 556-1140ms and 1387-2056ms. Nav animations begin at 361ms. Hero animations begin at 981ms, become running at 1121-1387ms and end at 2066-3059ms, so most of the intro falls inside the 433ms layout task and the 351ms script task. Deterministic check (blocktest2.js): I blocked the main thread for 700ms in the middle of the intro. Baseline presents 2 frames and the title changes in 1. With the move/blur split, 7-10 frames are presented and the title, sub and nav move in 6-8 of them.

rootCauses.claim: The brief says the hero has nested, simultaneous blurs. That is false. heroBlockIn (14px blur plus scale on .hero-inner) never runs. The comment that should start at styles.css:3607 has no '/*' opener, so the next rule's selector is invalid and the whole rule at styles.css:3616-3619 is dropped. Children blur on their own. This dead rule must NOT be repaired: repairing it would add a full-block blur that has never been in production, plus large paint cost.
rootCauses.evidence: getComputedStyle('.hero-inner').animationName is 'none' (probe.js). trace_warm has no Animation event for heroBlockIn. The layer list shows .hero-inner only with the 'Overlap' compositing reason. git log -L shows the opener has been missing since commit 6a8b0cf.

rootCauses.claim: The September claim that the collage rows exceed an 8192px GPU max texture size is overstated and not a real failure mode. The rows are composited layers about 9.2k px wide, but Chromium splits every such layer into tiles and only rasterizes tiles near the viewport. No texture ever spans the row's width. The real collage cost is GPU-process raster of 130 thumbnails, each with a paint-time filter including blur(2px), plus about 84 megapixels of composited layer area in total.
rootCauses.evidence: layers2.js lists 5 layers per row type: bg-row-track at 9214-9215x193 (draws nothing) and an 'Overlap' IMG drawing layer at 9226-9227x205. The root document layer (1440x6264) and MAIN (1440x5364) are also larger than 4096px and are tiled the same way. The cc trace shows per-tile RasterTask{tileData{layerId,tileId}} events and DidPrepareTiles with memory_limit_policy ALLOW_PREPAINT_ONLY and a 512MB hard limit. The only textures allocated at full size are render surfaces, and the rows' surfaces are clipped by .bg-row overflow:hidden to about 1594x193. 8192 is the limit on D3D10-class GPUs; D3D11 hardware allows 16384. The filter is set at styles.css:511, and RendererRasterWorker accounts for 713ms of GPU-process time in 0-3.5s across the whole page.

rootCauses.claim: On the GPU side, steady state draws 24 render passes per frame. 6 of them exist only because the intro animations use fill-mode 'both', which holds filter: blur(0) and opacity on 14 elements forever, and each held effect needs its own render pass. This cannot be removed without a visible change: the held values are relied on by the current look.
rootCauses.evidence: rpass.js (viz DirectRenderer::DrawRenderPass per DrawFrame): baseline 24, intro animations disabled 18. Switching the hero blur halves to fill 'backwards' only drops to 23. The nav animations hold opacity:1 and translate:0 forever. That overrides the brand/CTA opacity fade in the pill morph (styles.css:3033-3040) and the hover lift on nav links (translate at styles.css:3315). Releasing the fill would change those interactions, so I dropped this idea.

investigations.notes:
Result: paint and compositing are a secondary contributor to the entry jank. Layout, style and script long tasks dominate. My lane has two real, pixel-identical fixes:
(a) Stop the near-every-frame full re-layerization. This is measurable in FPS: about 5-8ms of each ~30ms frame at 4x from about 1.4s on and in steady state.
(b) Composite the intro's opacity and slide. This removes the visible slideshow effect, but rAF FPS will not show it.

Things for the orchestrator and other lanes:
1. bench.js 'layers' always returns 0 layers on Chrome 148. It sends LayerTree.enable before p.goto, and the agent is reset on navigation. Enable it after navigation; fixes/paint-composite/layers2.js does this. Real count is 172-175 layers and 84.4 megapixels. Layers over 4096px: the 5 row layers (about 9226x205), the root (1440x6264) and MAIN (1440x5364).
2. bench.js 'css' injection lands after the first style pass. Any variant that renames or replaces a running animation restarts it; I saw both the original and the new animation records in the trace. Use a 'files' override of /styles.css for such variants.
3. localhost:5173 was down for a stretch. I served the repo through in-browser request interception (fixes/paint-composite/bench_disk.js) and did not start any server. bench_disk.js also caps the lazy-image wait; bench.js has since been patched the same way. Final checks were rerun with the official bench.js after the server returned.
4. For the style-invalidation lane (isolated, CPU time per frame):
   - The .quote translate floats cost about 4ms of UpdateLayoutTree per frame (12.5ms wall at 4x), though they need no re-layerization.
   - The price-card floats cost about 1.4ms; btn-shiny's registered-property animation about 1.35ms.
   - When any main frame runs, every animated element (composited ones included) goes through style recalc.
5. For the offscreen-work lane: other off-screen animations still repaint on every frame: accent-soft orbs, chat pulseGreen and cfooter-center. They stay on the cheap repaint path. Pausing the price floats off-screen would also remove their cost, but changes their phase; my contain:paint fix needs no pause.
6. Do NOT repair the missing '/*' at styles.css:3607. heroBlockIn has never run in production, so repairing it would add a new effect.
7. Timing numbers here use thread CPU time (tdur) because the machine was at about 76% load from other agents. Wall-clock frame counts were too noisy to quote.

Helper scripts are in fixes/paint-composite/: vtrace.js (trace plus full-update counts), rpass.js (render passes per frame), ltchange.js (layer churn), blocktest2.js (smoothness during a forced main-thread block), vis_section.js and bandiff.js (below-the-fold identity), vis2.js (mobile and reduced-motion).

visualConcerns: Settled frames are identical. bench visual (my own copy of bench.js in the vet folder) showed 0 diff at 150/500/900/1400 ms. At 5000 ms the only diffs were in the hero counter strip (x 120-600, y 600-800), where baseline-vs-baseline also differs (counterSettle noise). I checked crops: same font, same text. This applies to the original proposal and to the amendment.

The proposer's claim that the hero text is never painted in a fallback font is contradicted by trace_cold.json. FCP is at 753 ms, but Inter Tight RemoteFontLoaded only lands at 1527 ms, followed by a 157 ms full relayout (1300/1372 objects) forced by script.js update@909. So on a cold first visit the H1 (heroTitleIn, 0.15 s delay + 1 s blur/fade) is drawn in system-ui/Segoe UI mid-fade and then swaps to Inter Tight, shifting the text. The fix removes that FOUT and layout shift. Nothing designed is removed, but what is drawn mid-intro does change, and the user should be told.

Chrome 148 holds the first paint for up to about 100 ms while an early-requested web font is still pending. Tiny-page test, font response delayed 2 s, median FCP minus DCL: 34 ms with no early request, 131 ms with a parser preload, 128 ms with a script-inserted preload, 131 ms with document.fonts.load. Real page, cold, gstatic delayed 1.5 s: median FCP 616 ms baseline vs 832 ms preload (noisy). When fonts come back fast there is no shift (cold, CPU 4x, paired medians 1132 ms baseline vs 820 ms preload). So on slow font fetches the first frame can appear up to about 100 ms later. CSS intro animations start at the first rendered frame, but the JS-timer-driven hero counters do not, so in that slow case their offset from the CSS animations can move by up to about 100 ms.

In the original proposal on Mac, iOS and Android, the 3 unused High-priority font downloads (about 124 KB) compete with styles.css and the 26 eager hero thumbnails. The real fonts and thumbnails can therefore land later than today on slow mobile links, making the FOUT and empty-thumbnail window longer. The amendment removes this.
breakages: Main defect: Google Fonts serves different woff2 URLs per user agent, and the 3 hardcoded URLs only match Chromium on Windows, Linux and ChromeOS (Chrome, Edge, Brave; also HeadlessChrome, so the bench cannot see the problem). I fetched the css2 URL with real UAs and got different latin files: ...SjIa1ZL7W0Q5nw / ...LsH8ahuQ2e8 / ...Dcwgknk-4 for macOS (Chrome, Safari, Firefox), iOS (Safari, CriOS), Android Chrome and Samsung Internet. Firefox on Windows gets a different Inter file (...W0I5nvwU). Opera / Opera GX gets static per-weight files. In puppeteer with a Pixel 8 UA and a Mac UA, the variant made 9 gstatic requests instead of 3. Result on those platforms: about 124 KB of unused downloads per first visit, an 'unused preload' console warning, no benefit, and the late-font full relayout still happens. 'Mobile layout' is on the must-keep list: it still works, but the fix makes it slower, not faster.

Version drift: if Google moves to newer versions than v9/v20/v24, desktop Chromium silently goes back to the late-font relayout and also pays the wasted downloads and the possible first-paint hold of up to about 100 ms. The proposer's 'nothing breaks' understates this.

No breakage found in the listed behaviours. Only head <link> tags change, so /#pricing landing, the live visits counter, the Discord ticket loop, reveal IntersectionObservers, the --fp footer, testimonial scroll, reduced motion, pointer parallax, lightbox and variant arrows are untouched. /tos/, /slots/ and 404 are untouched because they do not get the patch. The variant file keeps CRLF and UTF-8.
loading-font-preload.evidence: The mechanism holds on desktop Chromium. Orchestrator traces: in WARM, JetBrains Mono is requested at 523 ms (during the 433 ms layout), loads at 969 ms, and is followed by a 66 ms layout dirtying 1115/1176 objects at 977 ms (the 144 ms paint+layout task). In COLD, Inter Tight and JetBrains Mono load at about 1527 ms, followed by a 157 ms forced full relayout (1300/1372). I re-traced with my own script (vet/vtrace.js, files served by request interception because :5173 was down for part of the session; CPU 4x; Chrome 148), covering 6 preload runs (the proposal plus my amendment, cold and warm). In every one, the fonts were requested at 65-440 ms at High priority, there was no late RemoteFontLoaded (the fonts were used straight from memory), only one early font invalidation, and no full-page relayout after the fonts. Every baseline run had 1-2 such relayouts (1300/1372 objects). Expected gain: one long task of about 66-157 ms (at 4x) plus the full text repaint it triggers, out of about 1.5 s of entry long tasks. The 433 ms layout, the 350 ms script evaluation and the style recalcs stay. Impact is real but low-to-medium, roughly one fewer janky frame during the intro. Absolute timings on this machine were heavily contended, so I relied only on the order of events. The fatal problem is the UA-specific URLs, which I checked with curl and with puppeteer mobile/Mac UAs. Amended file: fixes/vet-loading-font-preload/index.uagated.html (built by make_amend.js in the same folder from the pristine repo file, CRLF). On HeadlessChrome/Windows it injects the 3 preloads (3 gstatic requests initiated by the script, no duplicates), gives the same trace ordering as the proposal, and bench visual is identical apart from the counter noise. Gate tested against 11 UAs; it preloads exactly where Google serves these URLs and skips Mac, iOS, Android, Firefox, Opera and Samsung. I also tried a URL-free alternative (document.fonts.load from the Google CSS link's onload). It is drift-proof but starts later, and one cold run still showed a late Inter load with a full relayout, so I am not recommending it as the primary fix.
loading-font-preload.amendment:
Do not ship the 3 parser-level <link rel=preload> tags. In index.html, right after line 26 (<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />) and before the fonts.googleapis.com css2 link, so that no stylesheet blocks it, insert a small inline script. It adds the same 3 preload links only when the browser is Chromium on Windows, Linux or ChromeOS, which are the only browsers Google sends these exact files to:

visualConcerns: The official bench cannot see this fix. bench.js visual calls a.pause() and sets currentTime, and pausing takes every animation off the compositor. Both variants are then drawn by the main thread, so the 0/0/0 result shows the computed values are equal and nothing more. The compositor path the fix relies on is never rendered in that test.

During every main-thread stall, the very condition the fix targets, the split draws frames that exist in neither the baseline nor the design. Opacity and slide keep advancing on the compositor while each blur stays at its value from the last main frame, so text shows up nearly fully opaque but heavily blurred, then snaps into focus when the next main frame arrives. In the design, high blur only ever occurs while opacity is low.

Warm trace (nav created at 361ms, main frame at 399ms, compositor drawing every 8ms from 556 to 1140ms during the 463+521ms long task). Split: the nav bar reaches 0.89-0.97 opacity with blur held at 10px (design at that moment: 0.3-1.1px), and the brand and links reach up to 0.92 opacity at 6px blur. Baseline: the nav stays invisible. Rendered: stack_navstallEnd.png.

Warm hero stall (main frames at 1388 and 1787ms, compositor drawing from 1408 to 1806ms). Split: subtitle at 0.91 opacity with 8px blur (design 0.7px), CTA at 0.75 with 8px (design 2px), title at 0.97 with 6px (design 0.3px). Rendered: stack_herostallEnd.png.

Cold first visit, the worst case: all intro animations stay pending on the main thread until 1967ms while the compositor draws continuously from 1529 to 2058ms. For about 0.5s the split shows the whole hero (title blurred 12px, sub/CTA/stats blurred 8px) and the nav (10px) at full opacity, then everything snaps sharp. Baseline shows an empty hero for that time, then pops in. Rendered: stack_cold.png.

Changes on an idle machine too, not only during stalls. I left the animations playing (playbackRate 1e-7) so the Move halves really run on the compositor; tracing confirmed Move halves compositeFailed=0 and Blur halves 4096. The split then differs from baseline at t=450/700/1000 by meanAbsDiff 0.20/0.24/0.10 (0.83/0.74/0.30% of pixels changed, max per-pixel difference 72-81), while the baseline-vs-baseline noise is exactly 0 at those times. paint-composite-intro-split.evidence:
VERDICT: drop. Nothing can rescue it: Chrome never composites a blur animation (compositeFailed=4096 means the filter may move pixels), so any split of blur from opacity/translate breaks them apart during stalls. That split is the whole source of the benefit, and also of the visual change.

1) VISUAL IDENTITY
- Official bench (fixes/vet-paint-composite-intro-split/visual_out.txt): 0/0/0 at 150/500/900/1400/5000 against noise 0-0.023. As expected, but this only proves the computed values match, because pause() takes every animation off the compositor.
- Stall frames (mixshot.js, mixshot2.js; results in mixshot_out.txt and the run log): I rendered the exact state each variant shows during a stall from the real traces. Baseline = everything frozen at t0. Split = Move halves at t1, Blur halves at t0.
  - Split stall frames match neither baseline (meanAbsDiff 4.5-18.4 in the nav and hero crops) nor design. Example: cold hero, split vs design 15.6 / 29.5% of pixels.
  - Control (split with every half at t1 vs design) = 0, so the method itself is sound.
  - In fairness, by pixel distance the split stall frame is somewhat closer to the design than the frozen baseline frame (cold hero 15.6 vs 18.5, nav 2.6 vs 6.4). But it is a state the design never has: opaque and blurred, followed by a focus snap from 8-12px to about 0.
  - The user's rule ("changes what is drawn ... at any moment, including mid-intro, is NOT acceptable") rules this out.
  - Side-by-side images: stack_navstallEnd.png, stack_herostallEnd.png, stack_cold.png.
- Idle machine with the compositor actually running (runshot.js, runshot_out.txt, run_heat_450.png, run_cmp_450.png; verifycomp.js confirmed Move halves cf=0 and Blur halves cf=4096 during the run): small but systematic subpixel text-rendering differences mid-intro, with A/A noise 0.

2) FUNCTIONAL SAFETY: no breakage found.
- No JS in the repo uses animationend/animationstart, getAnimations or animationName, so the renamed animations affect nothing.
- Reduced motion: the global !important duration rule applies to every entry in the list. The nav `animation: none` rule (L4070) still comes after the rewritten L4045/L4054, so it still wins.
- /tos/ keeps heroBadgeIn/heroTitleIn/heroFadeIn unchanged. .nav-back keeps navIn (the L4047 definition, which overrides L3285). /tos/ and /slots/ only get the split on .nav.
- Boot freeze uses a single animation-play-state value, which repeats over both halves; the splash is currently OFF.
- No html.lite rule touches these animations. The hash landing, counters, Discord loop, reveal observers, footer and testimonials don't depend on them.
- `fill: both` is kept, so the end state that the pill morph and hover depend on is held as before.
- Start-time sync is unchanged: in the baseline these animations already wait for the compositor start time, because they are batched with composited ambient animations (trace: cf0 animations in the same batch at 361/981ms).

3) MECHANISM: cosmetic. Zero main-thread work is removed. The long tasks (Layout 695ms, UpdateLayoutTree 585ms, EvaluateScript 368ms, Paint 356ms) are untouched, the Blur halves still need every main frame, and the accent rAF loop (script.js:937) keeps main frames going regardless. FPS and long-task metrics will not move; the author agrees. The compositor-advance effect itself is real (warm trace: compositor drew every 8ms during the 463+521 and 1421+351 tasks; cold: 1529-2058ms while the intro was still pending on main), but what it adds is exactly the mixed, out-of-design frames described above.

Considered and rejected amendment: compositing translate only, keeping opacity and blur together on main. It still decouples the properties during stalls (the slide runs ahead), it keeps the subpixel text difference, and it leaves almost no benefit.

Side note for other lanes: styles.css around L3606 has a comment with no opening `/*` ("HERO INTRO — zoom-out desfocado..."). It swallows the `.hero-inner { animation: heroBlockIn ... }` rule, so heroBlockIn never runs today. Do NOT "fix" that comment: doing so would add a new animation and change the visuals.
